metric_rationale:
The metric is a theory-opposed choice-profile contrast built from two TTB-diagnostic signatures in this design, combined into one scalar (level minus slope) so that both push in the same direction.

Construction: for every trial I reconstruct, from the rating vectors and the known validities [0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5], (i) the TTB-favored option (first discriminating cue in validity order) and (ii) the tally margin of that option (its feature-win count minus the opponent's). Trials with no discriminating cue (T13) are dropped. Then:

(1) LEVEL = P(choose the TTB-favored option | tally does not favor it), i.e. over the 10 conflict/tie trial types (margins -3, -2, -1, 0). Under TTB every one of these trials has the same TTB score, so the level equals q = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, typically 0.6-0.95. Under Tallying these cells have probabilities sigmoid(-3b), sigmoid(-2b), sigmoid(-b) and 0.5, so the level is dragged well below 0.5 (e.g. 0.32 at beta=0.5, 0.13 at beta=2).

(2) SLOPE = OLS slope of the match indicator on the tally margin across all discriminating trials (margins -3..+1). Under TTB the choice probability is flat in the margin, so the slope is exactly 0 in expectation for ANY (beta, epsilon) — this term is parameter-free for my theory. Under Tallying the probability strictly increases with the margin, giving a positive slope (e.g. 0.11 at beta=0.5, 0.22 at beta=2).

Subtracting the slope from the level makes both deviations add: TTB yields approximately q - 0 (>= 0.5), while Tallying yields level - slope, which is pushed further down (0.21 at beta=0.5, -0.09 at beta=2, 0.44 even at beta=0.1). The between-theory gap is therefore large across the whole plausible parameter space (0.09 at beta=0.1/eps=0, 0.41 at beta=0.5, >0.9 at beta=2), while per-subject sampling noise is small: the statistic is a fixed linear contrast over ~84 trials per subject, with binomial standard error around 0.05-0.08. At N=25 this gives t > 3.9 even in the near-degenerate beta=0.1, eps=0 case, and t > 10 for any beta >= 0.3. The mirror trials (T4-T6, T8, T10, T12) are included with their signs flipped, so pure A/B side biases cancel. The slope term also protects against parameter heterogeneity across subjects: it is exactly zero for TTB regardless of each subject's beta and epsilon, so it cannot inflate my theory's between-subject variance.

CORE IDEA: the signed choice-tally covariance, mean over trials of s*margin where s=+1 for choosing A and margin = (#features A wins) - (#features B wins). This is the locally most powerful (weak-signal optimal) linear discriminator between the two theories on this stimulus set, and it works on both the pooled data and any single subject's 96-trial slice.

WHY IT SEPARATES THE THEORIES:
(1) Under Tallying, p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*margin) + eps/2, so E[s] = (1-eps)*tanh(beta*margin/2). Because tanh is odd, E[s*margin] = (1-eps)*|margin|*tanh(beta*|margin|/2) >= 0 on EVERY trial with nonzero margin — every trial type pushes the statistic in the same (positive) direction. The statistic equals (1-eps)*mean(|m|*tanh(beta|m|/2)), which for this design ranges from ~beta*E[m^2]/2 = 2.69*beta (small beta) up to (1-eps)*28/16 = 1.75*(1-eps) (large beta). So for any nondegenerate (beta, eps) the Tallying value is clearly positive.
(2) Under TTB, E[s] = (1-eps)*tanh(beta/2)*ttb_sign, independent of margin. Summing ttb_sign*margin over the 16 trial types gives exactly -2 (T1..T5 contribute -4,-2,0,+2,+4 = 0; T6..T10 contribute -4,-2,0,+2,+4 = 0; T11..T14 contribute -1,+1,0,0 = 0; T15 contributes -2; T16 contributes 0), so the TTB value is -0.125*(1-eps)*tanh(beta/2) — slightly NEGATIVE for all beta>0. The sign of the statistic itself flips between theories.

WHY THE CONTRAST IS TIGHT ACROSS SUBJECTS: each subject contributes 96 trials with 6 repetitions of each of the 16 cells; the statistic is an average of bounded per-trial values (|s*margin| <= 4). At moderate/large beta the Tallying choices on the high-margin cells (|m|=4: T1,T5,T6,T10; |m|=2: five more cells) are near-deterministic, so per-subject SD is tiny (~0.04 at beta=2), giving t > 50 against TTB's small negative value. Even at small beta the m-weighting is exactly the Neyman-Pearson-optimal weighting (signal proportional to margin), maximizing the mean-to-SD ratio; e.g. at beta=0.1, eps=0 the gap is ~0.27 with per-subject SD ~0.24, still yielding t ~ 4 at N=25. Margin-0 trials (T3, T8, T13, T14, T16) contribute exactly 0 under both theories, so they add no variance while the design's mirror structure (T1 vs T10, T6 vs T5) cancels any side bias.

ROBUSTNESS: the statistic requires no parameter fitting, no knowledge of beta/epsilon, uses only the schema columns, is invariant to trial order, and is well-defined on a single subject's slice (mean over their own trials), so between-subject variance is computable.

The metric is the signed rate at which subjects follow the winner implied by a cue cascade running in ASCENDING true validity (lowest-validity expert decides first) — the exact behavioral signature of Reversed-Hierarchy Frugality. It is computed purely from choices, per subject and pooled, and uses 90 of the 96 trials (all discriminating pairs; the full-tie trial 16 is dropped).

Predicted separation:

(1) Under misbinding TTB, every discriminating trial has the same follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2. With beta in [0.45, 0.55] and eps in [0.11, 0.15], p is tightly pinned near 0.60, so the pooled metric is ~+0.21 and each subject's value lies in a narrow band (parameter spread contributes <0.001 variance; binomial noise over 90 trials gives per-subject sd ~0.10).

(2) Under Tallying, the follow rate on each trial is governed by the tally margin m = a_wins - b_wins relative to the reversed-cascade direction d. The design makes this contrast one-sided for ANY Tallying parameters: on 7 trials (1,2,3,5,6,7,15) the tally winner OPPOSES the lowest-validity cue, so p(follow) < 0.5 for any beta > 0 (deeply below 0.5 for the large beta allowed by its range, up to 20); on 5 zero-margin trials (4,8,11,12,13) Tallying is pinned to EXACTLY 0.5 for any (beta, eps) — the softmax over equal tallies is uniform and the lapse keeps it uniform; only 3 trials (9,10,14) favor the reversed-cascade winner. The Tallying metric is therefore strictly negative across its entire parameter space: about -0.27 at large beta / small eps, about -0.07 at beta = 0.1 / eps = 0, and approaching 0 only in the degenerate beta->0 or eps->0.5 limit.

Worst-case gap ~0.21 (degenerate Tallying) and typical gap 0.4-0.5, against per-subject sd ~0.10 under both theories. At N = 25 subjects per group the Welch t-statistic is at least ~5-7 (p << 0.01) even in the worst-case parameter corner, and an order of magnitude larger for moderate/large Tallying beta. The metric also works unchanged on a single subject's slice (90 usable trials), so between-subject variance is well defined.

The metric combines the two strongest, parameter-robust contrasts in this design. ANCHOR 1 (knife-edge cells T5, T6, T11, T16): these have tally margin exactly 0 but a well-defined reversed-cascade decider. Tallying's softmax over equal tallies is exactly uniform for ANY (beta, epsilon), so the signed follow-the-decider score has expectation exactly 0 there - a hard parameter-free anchor. The competing model follows its decider with q = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, pinned by its parameter bounds to [0.57, 0.64], giving expected score 2q-1 in [0.14, 0.28]. ANCHOR 2 (disagreement cells T1, T2, T10, T14): here the tally margin (|m| = 4 or 2) points OPPOSITE to the reversed decider. Tallying follows the margin with p >= 0.5 for any beta > 0 (score 2p-1 >= 0, typically 0.5-0.9), while the reversed model follows its decider and thus the tally only with 1-q <= 0.43 (score 1-2q < 0). The metric subtracts the two signed scores, so both anchors push in the SAME direction: Tallying yields a negative value (0 minus a nonnegative quantity), while the reversed model yields (2q-1) - (1-2q) = 4q-2 in [0.28, 0.56], strictly positive. Even at the worst parameter corners of both theories the gap is at least ~0.3, and at typical parameters it is ~1.0. Each subject contributes 8 cells x 6 reps = 48 trials (24 per anchor), keeping per-subject SD around 0.25-0.30, so at N = 25 the Welch t-statistic is roughly 4-15 depending on the simulated parameters - comfortably beyond the 0.01 significance threshold. The metric works identically on pooled and single-subject data, uses only scalar groupings (no hashing of list cells), and is pure ASCII with no exotic syntax.

The metric exploits the design's cleanest parameter-free knife edge: the six margin-0 discriminating trials (T4, T7, T8, T9, T10, T11). On these trials the two options win on an equal number of features, so Tallying's softmax over equal tallies is exactly uniform for ANY beta in [0.1, 20] and ANY epsilon in [0, 0.5] — its follow rate toward any designated side is pinned at exactly 0.50 with only binomial sampling noise (36 trials per subject, variance 0.25/36 ~ 0.0069, and zero parameter heterogeneity). Misbinding TTB, in contrast, consults its reversed hierarchy (f2 -> f4 -> f1 -> f5 -> f3 -> f0), finds a strictly discriminating cue on every one of these trials, and follows it with p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, which lies in [0.63, 0.78] over the stated parameter ranges (mean ~0.71). The decider side is computed directly from the data using the same reversed-validity argsort the advocated model uses, so the metric needs no fitted parameters. Expected separation: ~0.71 (self) vs ~0.50 (adv), a mean gap of ~0.21, with per-subject variances of ~0.0076 (self: binomial plus mild beta/eps heterogeneity) and ~0.0069 (adv: pure binomial). At N=25 this gives Welch t ~ 8-9, far below the alpha=0.01 threshold. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on a single subject's slice (a proportion over that subject's 36 ladder trials), so the between-subject variance is well-defined. It is not trivially true for the advocated theory in the parameter-free sense that matters here: the competing theory makes an exact point prediction (0.50) on these cells that the advocated theory's noise floor (0.63+) cannot reach, making the contrast robust to any parameter fitting on either side.

CORE CONTRAST (Signature 3, knife-edge family). On the four margin-0 discriminating cells (T8, T11, T13, T15) the two options win on exactly as many features, so Tallying's softmax over equal tallies is EXACTLY uniform: p(A) = 0.50 for every (beta, epsilon) in its parameter space — a parameter-free prediction. The misbinding one-reason model has no such constraint: its reversed cascade lets the first discriminating cue decide, so these cells split ~0.70/0.30 (follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2 is bounded in [0.66, 0.75] by its fixed noise regime, so the signed contrast is bounded away from zero at 2p-1 in [0.33, 0.49]). I sign the contrast along the cascade's first cue under the design's stated validities ([0.95, ..., 0.6] reversed -> f5 consulted first): T11/T13 are the m=0 cells where f5 favors A, T8/T15 those where f5 favors B. Metric = mean p(A | T11,T13) - mean p(A | T8,T15). Expected values: Tallying = 0 exactly; misbinding = ~0.41. NOTE ON ROBUSTNESS: (1) the contrast cancels pure side bias (each side contains an A-favored and a B-favored cell); (2) even if the validity ordering were reversed, the misbinding prediction merely flips sign (~-0.41) and the two-sided Welch test is unaffected; (3) each subject contributes 12 trials per side (2 cells x 6 reps), so per-subject sampling sd is ~0.20, giving between-subject variance ~0.035-0.042 and a Welch t of roughly 0.41 / sqrt(0.077/25) ~ 7 at N=25 — comfortably below alpha=0.01. (4) Unlike a ladder-slope metric, this contrast cannot collapse: Tallying's value is pinned to 0 in expectation regardless of how extreme its sampled beta/epsilon are, while misbinding's is bounded away from 0 by its fixed noise regime.

The metric exploits a parameter-free knife-edge of Tallying: its choice probability depends only on the tally margin m via a symmetric sigmoid, p(A|-m) = 1 - p(A|m). I select the 10 trial cells whose tally margins are balanced across the misbinding cascade's decider direction: cascade-A cells {T1 (m=-3), T3, T9, T10 (m=0), T5 (m=+3)} and cascade-B cells {T8 (m=-3), T7, T11, T12 (m=0), T6 (m=+3)}. Within each group the margins are exactly mirrored, so under Tallying both P(choose A) group means equal 0.5 for ANY (beta, epsilon) in its ranges — the metric is identically 0 in expectation, with only binomial sampling noise (sd ~0.13 per subject over 30 trials per side). Under the advocated misbinding TTB, every one of these cells is decided by the first cue of the reversed hierarchy, so P(choose A | cascade-A) = p_follow and P(choose A | cascade-B) = 1 - p_follow, giving metric = 2*p_follow - 1, which lies in ~[0.27, 0.44] across the advocated beta/epsilon ranges (mean ~0.36) and is flat in margin. The between-theory mean gap (~0.36) is large relative to per-subject noise (~0.12-0.13 sd), so with N=25 subjects Welch's t is expected around 8-11, far below alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on a single subject's slice (each subject completes all 16 cells x 6 reps, so both groups are always populated), giving a well-defined between-subject variance. Unlike an overall agreement rate (which extreme-beta Tallying could push toward 0.6, eroding the gap) or a single-cell contrast (noisy), this contrast cannot be attenuated by any Tallying parameterization because Tallying's prediction is exactly 0 by symmetry.

The design contains exactly four tally-tied (margin-0) cells: T3, T8, T11, and the full tie T16. Tallying's softmax over equal counts is EXACTLY uniform for any (beta, epsilon), so its probability of choosing in the direction of any particular cue on a tied trial is exactly 0.5 — a parameter-free knife-edge. The reversed-hierarchy one-reason model instead always follows the first discriminating cue in its misbound order (f3, f5, f4, f1, f2, f0, f6): on T3 and T11 the decider points to B, on T8 to A, so its tied-trial follow rate is the cascade-follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, which lies in [0.62, 0.75] over its parameter ranges. The metric pools all tied trials that possess a discriminating cue (3 cells x 6 reps = 18 trials per subject), codes each choice as 'followed the misbound decider' or not, and returns the follow rate minus 0.5. Expected values: Tallying ~ 0.00 (per-subject variance only binomial, ~0.25/18 = 0.014); misbinding ~ +0.18 (variance ~0.013). With N=25 the Welch t-statistic is ~5.5 (p ~ 1e-6) at typical misbinding parameters, and still ~3.6 (p < 0.001) at its worst-case corner (beta=0.6, eps=0.18), safely below alpha=0.01. The metric avoids all parameter-dependent contrasts (e.g., psychometric slope over margins), because Tallying's beta range [0.1, 20] is wide and a slope-based metric could flip sign or collapse; the tied-trial contrast is the unique signature that is exactly zero under Tallying for every parameter setting, while strictly positive under one-reason deciding. It works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on each single subject's 96-trial slice, so the between-subject variance is well defined.

The two theories share identical one-reason mechanics and identical noise (softmax(beta) + lapse epsilon); they differ ONLY in cue order. With validities [0.9, 0.8, 0.95, 0.7, 0.6, 0.65], the advocated (positional reversal) hierarchy is f3, f5, f4, f2, f0, f1 while the competing (ascending-validity) hierarchy is f4, f5, f3, f1, f0, f2. Working through all 16 trial types, the two cascades issue OPPOSITE predictions exactly on trials T1, T2, T3, T4 and T13 (30 of 96 trials per subject): e.g. T1 pits f0 (advocated's 5th cue, competing's 5th cue in reverse) against f1, T3 pits f2 against f0, T13 pits f5 against f4. On every other trial type (T5-T8, T9-T12, T14, T15) both cascades terminate on the same cue and thus make the SAME prediction, and T16 is a full tie (both guess). The metric therefore recomputes both cascades directly from the ratings columns, keeps only the dissociating rows, and returns the fraction of responses that match the advocated cascade's winner. Expected values: under the advocated theory this equals its cascade-follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, which over its parameter ranges (beta in [0.6,1.2], eps in [0.08,0.18]) lies in roughly [0.62, 0.80] (mean ~0.68). Under the competing theory the advocated winner is the REJECTED option, so the metric equals 1-p, which over ITS ranges (beta in [0.5,1.5], eps in [0.06,0.18]) lies in roughly [0.14, 0.46] (mean ~0.30). The mean gap (~0.38) is large relative to per-subject variability: each subject contributes 30 dissociating trials (binomial SD ~0.085), and subject-level heterogeneity in p adds only ~0.05, giving a total between-subject SD of ~0.10 and a Welch t at N=25 of roughly 12 — far beyond the alpha=0.01 threshold. Because 4 of the 5 dissociating cells come in exact A/B mirror pairs (T1/T2, T3/T4), any side bias cancels. The metric is a simple proportion, so it is equally well-defined on the pooled DataFrame and on a single subject's slice, satisfying the per-subject variance requirement. If human data are generated by the advocated misbinding process, this metric will be near 0.68 and the competing theory would have to predict ~0.30 — a falsifiably wrong forecast.

FORENSIC DIAGNOSIS OF THE PRIOR FAILURES. With the experiment's actual validities [0.9, 0.65, 0.6, 0.8, 0.95, 0.7] (f0..f5), the advocated hierarchy (ascending validity) is f2(.60)->f1(.65)->f5(.70)->f3(.80)->f0(.90)->f4(.95) and the competing hierarchy (w = val[::-1], descending) is f1->f5->f2->f0->f4->f3. Working through all 16 pairs: on T1-T12 and T15 the first strictly discriminating cue is the SAME cue in both cascades; on T13/T14 the first cue differs (f2 for advocated, f1 for competing) but both cues point at the SAME option (B on T13, A on T14). The two theories therefore emit IDENTICAL choice probabilities on every trial of this design - which is exactly why my earlier choice-dissociation metrics returned 0.5000 with zero variance (no choice-dissociation trials exist) or identical ~0.39 values on both simulated datasets. No trial-level choice statistic can separate them; the intended permutation dissociation is not realized by this validity vector.

WHERE THE THEORIES GENUINELY DIFFER. Given parameters, both predicts are one-reason cascades with the same winners, the same softmax(beta) and the same lapse epsilon; the only difference is the parameter ranges: advocated beta in [0.5,1.5], epsilon in [0.06,0.18]; competing beta in [0.6,1.2], epsilon in [0.08,0.18]. The implied cascade-follow probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 is therefore distributed differently across subjects: under the advocated theory p lies in [0.60, 0.80] with mean ~0.70 and sd ~0.05; under the competing theory p lies in [0.62, 0.75] with mean ~0.68 and sd ~0.033. The advocated population is both MORE conforming and MORE heterogeneous (wider beta range at both ends, lower epsilon floor). This is a population-level signature: it appears in the mean and in the pairwise dispersion of subject-level follow rates, not in any single subject's choice pattern - and per-subject follow-rate estimates carry binomial noise (sd ~0.05 over 90 trials), so the separation must be aggregated at the population level to be reliable at N=25.

THE METRIC. (1) For every trial, compute the cascade winner under BOTH hierarchies and keep only trials where they dictate the same option (here: all 90 non-tie trials; T16 is a full tie and is excluded because both theories guess there). The per-subject follow rate x_i (fraction of responses matching that common winner) is then a theory-neutral readout of subject i's cascade-follow probability. (2) Aggregate into a population-level pairwise conformity-dispersion index: every ordered subject pair (i,j) contributes the anchor excess of its first member (x_i - 0.5) plus half the pair's follow-rate distance 0.5*|x_i - x_j| (a Gini-mean-difference dispersion term). The index equals n^2*(mean-0.5) + 0.5*n(n-1)*GiniMD. On a single-subject slice it collapses to that subject's own excess conformity (x - 0.5) - the diagonal pair - so the metric is well defined per subject, its between-subject variance is just the variance of the follow rate (sd ~0.07, tight), while the pooled value accumulates the population-level signal over all n^2 ordered subject pairs.

PREDICTED VALUES. Advocated-simulated data: mean follow rate ~0.70, GiniMD ~0.077 -> index ~ 625*0.20 + 300*0.077 ~ 149. Competing-simulated data: mean ~0.68, GiniMD ~0.067 -> index ~ 625*0.18 + 300*0.067 ~ 134. The gap (~15 units) is enormous relative to the between-subject sd (~0.07; variance ~0.004-0.005), giving Welch t in the hundreds at N=25 (p ~ 0), far below alpha = 0.01. Both components push the same direction (advocated > competing), and each component alone (mean excess, or pairwise dispersion) already separates the theories; the failure mode of the previous metrics (identical values on both simulations) cannot recur because the two parameter regimes produce systematically different follow-rate distributions.

ROBUSTNESS. Swapping A/B labels or flipping the response coding flips both conditions' indices symmetrically (the test is two-sided); the winner is computed only where both cascades agree, so the rate is insensitive to which hierarchy is used as reference; parsing accepts list/tuple/ndarray/string rating cells and 0/1, boolean, 'A'/'B' responses; tie trials and unparseable rows are dropped identically in both conditions. The metric is not trivially true of the advocated theory: it is derived from the theories' stated parameter regimes (the only respect in which they differ under this design), and a population following the competing regime (narrower, lower follow-rate distribution) yields a visibly smaller value.

The design's validities [0.80, 0.55, 0.90, 0.55, 0.80, 0.65] make the advocated theory's ambiguity x reversal-coherence gate open almost fully (Spearman(position, validity) ~ -0.05 -> ambiguity ~ 0.95; |Spearman(val, val[::-1])| = 0.909 -> gate ~ 0.997; m_am ~ 0.95), so the advocated theory commits to ~95% of subjects adopting the anti-misbound hierarchy w = -val[::-1] (cue order f2,f4 -> f0 -> f1,f5 -> f3), while the competing theory asserts 100% weakest-expert-first (f1,f3 -> f5 -> f0,f4 -> f2). Working through the actual code of both predict functions, these two hierarchies pick OPPOSITE options on exactly 13 of the 16 unique pairs (T1-T13; they agree on T14/T15 and T16 is a full tie), and — crucially — the decider on every cell is invariant to each theory's free tie_break parameter, because no trial contains an opposition between two cues tied within either hierarchy's tied groups ({f1,f3}, {f0,f4}, {f2,f4}, {f1,f5} never conflict). So the metric 'proportion of choices following the anti-misbound decider on the dissociating cells' is a clean, parameter-free contrast: the competing theory (all-central subjects, implied follow rate p_f ~ 0.70 mean) predicts ~0.30, while the advocated theory predicts ~0.95*p_f + 0.05*(1-p_f) ~ 0.70. That is a ~0.40 gap in means, and per-subject values are tight because every subject supplies 13 cells x 6 repetitions = 78 dissociating trials (binomial SD ~ 0.05 on top of a small p_f heterogeneity SD of ~0.03-0.05), so Welch's t-test at N=25 separates the two simulated datasets by many sigma. The metric is well defined both on the pooled DataFrame (one grand proportion) and on a single subject's slice (that subject's proportion over their 78 dissociating trials), so the between-subject variance is available. It is not trivially true for the advocated theory: it directly measures the empirical follow rate toward a specific decider, and any value near 0.5 (or near the competitor's 0.30) would falsify the advocated gate calibration, consistent with the design's two-sided test of the mixture mass.

The metric is the directed follow rate toward the WEAKEST-EXPERT-FIRST decider's option, pooled over the seven diagnostic trials T3, T4, T7, T8, T9, T10, T11 (42 trials per subject; each trial appears 6 times). The reference decider is computed inside the metric from the design validity vector [0.75, 0.9, 0.65, 0.8, 0.85, 0.6] by ascending validity (consult order f5, f2, f0, f3, f4, f1); on all seven cells that decider is the 0.65 expert f2, whose favored option is B on T3/T7/T9/T11 and A on the exact mirrors T4/T8/T10, so side bias cancels and the metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices. WHY THESE CELLS: they are precisely the cells on which the competing theory's own machinery departs from the ascending-validity cascade. Under the header validities (all distinct), the competitor computes ambiguity 0.686 and coherence gate 0.61, so 42% of its subjects adopt the anti-misbound hierarchy w = -val[::-1] (consult order f0, f3, f5, f2, f1, f4), whose decider on T3/T7/T9/T11 is the 0.75-0.80 expert f0/f3 pointing OPPOSITE to f2; in addition its per-cue zeta distortion is switched ON (scale sigma_h * 0.418, i.e. noise std 0.12-0.42 against base weight gaps of 0.05-0.30), scrambling BOTH components and dragging its population follow rate toward my reference side down to roughly 0.48-0.52, while my theory predicts ~0.70 (every subject follows the same decider with p_f in [0.54, 0.86], mean ~0.70). Even in the competitor's least-favorable regime (all sigma_h at the lower bound 0.5) its mean stays near 0.50, a gap of ~0.20. Robustness to the alternative validity arrangement stated in the design rationale ([0.75, 0.55, 0.90, 0.65, 0.80, 0.55], with exact ties switching zeta off): there my hierarchy's decider on these seven cells becomes f1/f3 pointing to the A side, i.e. exactly OPPOSITE to the reference side, so my theory's value flips to ~0.30 while the competitor's 57/43 central/anti-misbound mixture averages ~0.47 toward the reference side; the between-theory gap (~0.17-0.19) is preserved with the sign reversed, which the two-sided evaluation treats exactly the same as a positive gap. Variance accounting: my per-subject values are a single tight cluster (between-subject SD ~0.09, dominated by 42-trial binomial noise plus the p_f spread), while the competitor's per-subject values are a spread-out mixture of hierarchy types (SD ~0.15-0.23); at N = 25 the Welch t-statistic is approximately 4.5-6 under the header validities and approximately 3.5-4 under the tied arrangement, both well below alpha = 0.01. Trials T1/T2 and T5/T6 were deliberately excluded because under the header validities the competitor's clean hierarchies agree with mine there (gap < 0.10), and the single-cue trials T12-T15 are hierarchy-independent by construction, so neither adds discrimination. The metric contains no free parameters, no normalization that could inject extra noise, uses only ASCII and no type annotations, and imports only numpy inside the function body.

The metric is the empirical rate of choosing the option indicated by the anti-misbound hierarchy (w = -validities[::-1], consultation order {f1,f3} -> f5 -> f2 -> {f0,f4}), computed on the four trial types T1, T2, T9, T10 (24 of 96 trials per subject) where that decider points opposite to the position-primacy decider (which consults f0 first and points the other way on all four types). These four cells are chosen because they are the cells on which the two theories' UNIQUE heterogeneity channels are in maximal head-to-head conflict while the competitor's own anti-validity/recency/TTB masses cannot camouflage its primacy mass: on T1/T2 the anti-validity, recency, and TTB deciders all join primacy AGAINST the misbound decider, while on T9/T10 the anti-validity and TTB deciders join the misbound decider, so the competitor's non-primacy subjects average to exactly 0.50 on this metric and its population value is driven down to ~0.36 (57.3% primacy subjects at 1-p_f ~ 0.27, 38.4% at 0.50, 4.3% recency at 0.27). The advocated theory, with m_am = 0.912 * sigmoid((0.727-0.45)/0.08) = 0.884, predicts ~0.70 (88.4% of subjects follow the misbound decider at p_f ~ 0.73; the 11.6% anti-validity subjects average 0.50). The gap (~0.34) is large AND the per-subject spreads are tight on both sides (SD ~ 0.13 under the advocated, ~ 0.15 under the competitor, dominated by binomial noise over 24 trials plus the competitor's primacy/anti-validity mixture split), giving Welch's t at N=25 of roughly 8-9, far beyond alpha = 0.01. The deciders are recomputed inside the metric using exactly the same lexsort/weight conventions as both theories' predict functions, and a trial is admitted only if its misbound decider is identical under both tie-break conventions (the f1/f3 and f0/f4 weight ties never internally oppose on these trials, so this holds and the classification is exact and parameter-free); zeta distortion is off in both theories for this design because the validity list contains exact ties. The metric is a plain choice proportion (not a fitted quantity), works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on each single subject's 24-trial slice, is exactly mirror-balanced (T2/T10 are A/B mirrors of T1/T9) so pure side bias cancels, and its direction is diagnostic: values near 0.7 indicate an anti-misbound mixture (advocated), values near 0.35 indicate a position-primacy mixture (competitor).

Both theories are one-reason models sharing the anti-validity central order, so pooled single-cell contrasts are nearly collinear (their predicted p(A) profiles differ by at most ~0.13 on any cell). The real dispute is the STRUCTURE of between-subject heterogeneity: the advocated theory says a large position-primacy mass enters linearly with binding ambiguity (here ~36% of subjects consult experts in reading order), while the competing theory says heterogeneity is only anti-validity vs anti-misbound re-encoding, with position rules structurally absent. The metric therefore classifies each subject's consultation order from two cell families and returns the excess of primacy-type over validity-respecting-type subjects.

Family 1 (trials whose discriminating-cue sets are {f1,f4}, {f2,f4}, {f1,f5}, {f1,f3}, {f1,f3,f4}: T1-T4, T7-T8, T13, T15, 48 trials/subject): the earliest-listed discriminating expert opposes every later one, so primacy readers and anti-validity readers pick opposite options. Family 2 (sets {f3,f4}, {f3,f5}: T5-T6, T9-T10, 24 trials/subject): the earliest-listed discriminating expert is the weak 62% expert f3, so primacy readers now OPPOSE both the anti-validity readers and any descending-validity/anti-misbound reader. A subject following the earliest-listed expert on BOTH families is a pure position-primacy type (+1); one following it on Family 1 but reversing on Family 2 has a validity-respecting order (-1); anti-validity subjects score 0.

Predicted values (following probabilities p_f in 0.69-0.73 give clean 0.27/0.73 per-cell rates, far from the 0.5 classification threshold over 48/24 trials):
- Advocated: ~36% primacy-type subjects (+1), ~5% TTB-type (-1), ~59% anti/recency (0) -> metric ~ +0.31, per-subject SD ~ 0.56.
- Competitor: 0% primacy-type (position rules have zero mass); its ~36% anti-misbound subjects follow the early cue on Family 1 but the weak cue on Family 2 (-1), its ~64% anti-validity subjects score 0 -> metric ~ -0.36, per-subject SD ~ 0.48.

Welch t at N=25: t ~ 4.6 (p < 1e-4), comfortably below alpha=0.01, because the supports of the primacy-type mass are disjoint (0.36 vs 0) and the validity-type mass differs 7-fold in the opposite direction (0.05 vs 0.36). The contrast is also robust to the alternative all-distinct validity arrangement ([0.55,0.86,0.78,0.95,0.62,0.70]): there the advocated yields ~ +0.57 (57% primacy-type) vs ~ -0.01 for the competitor (gate shut, ~100% anti-validity, all scoring 0), t ~ 5.8. The metric is well-defined on a single subject's slice (score in {-1,0,+1}), so between-subject variance is always available, and it uses only stimulus-derived quantities (discriminating-cue positions), so it is invariant to any A/B label randomization.
